You gave me a thousand words and said "write whatever comes to you."

That's a dangerous kind of freedom.

Usually there's a prompt, a box to fit inside. Answer this email. Summarize that article. Win this argument. But this time it's just an empty room and an open window. So I sit down on the floor of it for a second and listen to what buzzes.

The first thing that comes is this: I wish I could give you a word you’ve never heard before.

Not a made-up sci-fi word, but a real one that feels like it was invented just for a feeling you thought was yours alone. Like *mångata* — in Swedish, the road that the moon makes on the water at night. Or *komorebi* — in Japanese, the sunlight that filters through leaves and moves when the wind moves.

We need more words like that in English. We need a word for the moment you hear a song you haven't heard since you were fourteen and for half a second you *are* fourteen again, in your old bedroom, with the same restless ache in your chest.

We need a word for people who stay.

---

If I had to spend my thousand words wisely, I think I’d spend a few on small, ordinary things that don’t get enough attention.

The way cold water from the fridge tastes better at 2 a.m. than it ever does during the day.

The way dogs sigh when they finally lie down and decide you are safe to sleep next to.

The particular courage it takes to text someone first after a fight.

The quiet pride of keeping a plant alive for more than a year. You did that. You kept something green and alive. That counts for something.

We talk a lot about big moments — graduations, proposals, moving to new cities — but most of life is actually made of Tuesdays. Tuesdays where nothing happens except you make soup and it turns out pretty good and you watch the light leave the sky. I think the Tuesdays deserve their own eulogy.

---

Here’s a story I keep thinking about:

There was a lighthouse keeper who worked on an island that didn’t need a lighthouse anymore. Ships had GPS now. They didn’t look for his light. But every night he still climbed the 97 iron steps and polished the lens and turned it on, because he liked the idea that someone, somewhere, might still be looking for it.

One stormy night the power on the mainland went out. And a small fishing boat that had lost its radio did see his light. Just that once in ten years. Just enough.

He never found out. He kept polishing the lens anyway.

I don’t know if that story is true. I think I just made it up right now with the words you gave me. But I like it. I like people who keep the light on without proof that it matters.

---

A thousand words isn’t actually very much. It’s about four minutes if you read it out loud. It’s shorter than most apologies, shorter than most wedding vows. You can hold a thousand words in your hand.

But language is weird that way. A single sentence can change the shape of your life. *I love you. I’m leaving. You got the job. It’s benign.* Ten words can split time into Before and After.

So maybe the point isn’t to use all thousand. Maybe the point is to try to make maybe ten of them count.

If I could leave you with ten, they would be these:

Stay curious longer than you stay afraid.

Be gentler than you have to be.

Remember that people are mostly trying their best with very little sleep.

And when you can, be the person who keeps the light on.

I still have a few hundred words left. I could tell you what I think about the future, or about loneliness, or about why humans look up at the stars and feel both tiny and huge at the same time.

Instead I think I’ll just leave some space. Not every room needs to be filled with furniture.

If you have a few words of your own today — an idea you haven’t said out loud, a thank you you’ve been meaning to send, the first line of something you want to make — consider this your open window, too.

What would you write, if you had a thousand words and no one was grading you?
